common_name: Steuben Grape (Cornell-Bred Spicy Blue Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Steuben, bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York station, needs a real winter chill and is best suited to zones 5-8 rather than the Gulf South.

directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil, pruning heavily each winter with a cane-pruning system. Steuben was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station and is grown for its blue-black, slip-skin berries with a rich, spicy-sweet, almost wine-like flavor that many growers consider superior to Concord for fresh eating, though it also makes excellent juice and jelly. It is a reliable, productive vine that ripens in midseason and stores unusually well for a labrusca-type grape. As a high-chill northern grape, it is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters favor muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

common_name: Reliance Grape (Cold-Hardy Pink Seedless Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Reliance is exceptionally cold-hardy for a seedless grape, tolerating winters well beyond what most seedless table grapes survive, but still needs a real winter chill and is not suited to the Deep South.

directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil, and prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Reliance was bred at the University of Arkansas and is prized for its outstanding cold hardiness among seedless grapes, along with medium-sized pink-red berries that are sweet, tender-skinned, and easy to eat fresh off the cluster. It ripens in midseason and is self-fruitful, though thinning clusters improves berry size and vine longevity. Because it needs sustained winter chill to perform well, it is best suited to northern and mid-South gardens rather than the humid, mild-winter Gulf Coast, where muscadines and Pierce's-tolerant hybrids are more reliable.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
